title: Arrangements: Partitions, Zones, And Duality
notes: Open by presenting arrangements as the chapter's common data structure. A set of lines cuts the plane into vertices, edges, and faces; the zone theorem explains why one insertion is local; and duality turns point questions into searches through levels. Keep the provenance explicit: printed pages 193-219 correspond to PDF pages 202-228.

title: Why Arrangements: Cell Partition Visual
notes: Use the cell partition image as the first mental model. The arrangement is not just a drawing of lines; it is a searchable subdivision where every cell has the same combinatorial relationship to the input lines. This is why later visibility, graphics, Voronoi, and optimization problems can all be phrased as finding or walking cells.

title: Simple Arrangement Counts
notes: Read the three formulas as a ledger that only works under simple-position assumptions. Every pair of lines contributes exactly one vertex, each line is cut into n edges, and Euler's planar bookkeeping gives the face count. The notebook check fixes n at six and verifies fifteen vertices, thirty-six edges, and twenty-two faces.

title: Degeneracy Is Cheaper
notes: Make the phrase cheaper precise: parallel lines and triple intersections merge events that would be separate in a simple arrangement. The left picture has fewer vertices because several incidences collapse together. A small perturbation separates them, raising the count back to the simple maximum, which explains why worst-case proofs usually assume general position first.

title: The Zone Of A Line
notes: Define the zone operationally. If a new line h is inserted into an existing arrangement, the zone is the sequence of cells crossed by h, together with the boundary edges of those cells. The figure's crossing order and edge proxy are small enough to inspect, while the theorem promises that this local walk remains linear in n.

title: Zone Theorem Proof Roadmap
notes: This slide is a proof map, not a full proof. The important idea is to charge boundary edges of crossed cells to nearby crossings and to separate edges above and below the inserted line. Because a line can enter the zone only through controlled local events, the total charge grows linearly rather than quadratically.

title: Incremental Construction
notes: Translate the theorem into an algorithm. Maintain the current planar subdivision, insert the next line, walk its zone, split the crossed cells, and update adjacency along the walk. The theorem is doing the performance work: it says each insertion touches only linear complexity in the number of lines already present.

title: Quadratic Cost Ledger
notes: Use the ledger to make the asymptotic sum concrete. The kth insertion sees at most a constant times k existing lines, so the cumulative upper bound is a triangular sum. The notebook table records the sequence zero, six, eighteen, thirty-six, sixty, ninety for six insertions under the source's six-n zone bound.

title: Higher Dimensions
notes: Generalize carefully. In d dimensions, arrangements of hyperplanes can have order n to the d cells, while the zone of one hyperplane has one lower dimension of complexity. The slide's cube-and-planes sketch is meant to preserve the same story: full arrangements are large, but one insertion sees a codimension-one boundary.

title: Duality Setup
notes: Introduce duality as an incidence-preserving translation, not as algebra for its own sake. A point becomes a line, and the question of whether a primal point lies above a primal line turns into an above-below relation in the dual arrangement. This is the doorway from point problems to level searches.

title: Levels As Search Objects
notes: A level is the curve through arrangement edges with a fixed number of lines below it. Median levels are especially useful because they encode balanced cuts. Use the notebook's duality check to connect the crossing of two median levels to a ham-sandwich line that bisects two odd point sets.

title: Higher-Order Voronoi
notes: Connect the new chapter back to Voronoi diagrams. Ordinary nearest-neighbor cells are order-one regions; higher-order cells ask for the same k nearest sites. In the lifted or dual view, that question becomes a level or envelope search, so arrangements give a uniform way to organize order-k nearest-neighbor structure.

title: Ham-Sandwich Via Median Levels
notes: Treat the ham-sandwich result as the most memorable duality payoff. In the primal plane, we seek one line that bisects two point sets. In the dual arrangement, each set contributes a median level, and an intersection of those levels maps back to the desired bisecting line.

title: Applications Map
notes: Use the application map to keep the chapter from feeling like a single theorem. The same arrangement vocabulary supports endpoint visibility, hidden-surface removal, aspect graph changes, shadow directions, red-blue matching, centerpoints, and minimum-area triangle searches. The point is transfer: once the subdivision is built, many geometric questions become location or traversal tasks.

title: Failure Modes And Assumptions
notes: Pause on assumptions before the recap. Simple arrangements remove parallelism and triple intersections, duality needs a convention for vertical lines and points at infinity, and numeric code must decide how to handle nearly coincident events. These are not afterthoughts; they determine whether the combinatorial ledger matches the computed subdivision.

title: Recap And Inspection Prompt
notes: Close by asking students to inspect a small arrangement rather than merely repeat definitions. They should identify the counts, trace one inserted line's zone, explain why the total incremental cost is quadratic, and describe how a point-set problem becomes a level query under duality. That sequence is the chapter's conceptual spine.
